messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I am brand-new to ERGMs, having recently made the jump from Siena models, so this question is very rudimentary. I?ve worked through a handful of the (very helpful) tutorials and am still unclear, so I figured I?d give this group a try.

I am interested in modeling nodal in-degree and out-degree based on a specific attribute. For example, a binary indicator of diabetes. I am theoretically interested in the association between diabetes status (with or without) and both outgoing and incoming friendship nominations. In following David Schaefer?s 2014 obesity paper in the American Journal of Public Health, I am hoping to model indegree, outdegree, and homophily based on this attribute in order to parse apart concepts such as social withdrawal and social marginalization. 

Any feedback on the correct term is appreciated. 

All the best,

Emily

Emily Long
Doctoral Candidate
Prevention Science Lab
Department of Psychology
Utah State University

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Basic attribute-based indegree/outdegree
messages.body_plain:
Welcome Emily!

If I understand you correctly, you are interested in different attribute 
groups having different mean in-degrees from each other, and different 
mean out-degrees from each other, as well as homophily.? If that is the 
case, and the attributes are categorical, then the terms to use are 
nodeifactor, nodeofactor and nodematch.

If the attribute in question is quantitative rather than categorical, 
then nodeicov, nodeocov, and absdiff may be what you want.

If you want to do more specific degree models (i.e. a propensity for 
nodes with a particular attribute to have exactly in-degree 1, or 
something like that), then you can use the terms idegree and odegree.

More information on each of these, and the arguments they take, can be 
found at help("ergm-terms")

Cheers,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] 3 terms nodefactor
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

 

I am trying to fit a one-off relationship network (Adaptation of S. Goodreau
and S. Jeness work in racial disparities among MSM in Atlanta work (Lancet
2017)). 

I want my network to be influenced by the sex (sex; 'M', 'W'), the number of
main relationship (deg.main; 0, 1) and the number of casual relationship
(deg.pers; 0, 1, 2) of individuals.

 

My formation formulae is then (I have removed all the terms we are not
interested in here):

 

formation.i <- ~ edges + nodefactor(c('sex',"deg.main", "deg.pers"), base =
1)

 

I was expected to give a length 12 target statistic vector :

-          1 for edges count 

-          2 (sex levels)   x   2 (deg.main levels)   x 3 (deg.pers levels)
- 1 (ref level here sex: M , deg.main: 0, deg.pers: 0 ) = 11 paramters

 

But the model (netest) keep complaining requiring for 11 parameters only.

 

Here is the error message:

 

--

Error in vector.namesmatch(target.stats, names(nw.stats)) : 

  Length of "target.stats" is 12 but should be 11.

--

 

Does somebody know why nodefactor(c('sex',"deg.main", "deg.pers"), base = 1)
requires only 10 parameters (and not 11 i.e. 12 combinations of sex,
deg.main, deg.pers - 1 ref level)?

 

Best,

Damien

messages.subject: [statnet_help] 3 terms nodefactor
messages.body_plain:
Damien -

My guess is that in the network that you created to do the estimation 
on, one of the 12 possible (sex x deg.main x deg.pers) combinations is 
not actually represented by anybody in the network.? The tools can't 
tell that there are some combinations that are theoretically possible in 
your model but don't actually appear, so they don't include a term for them.

If you check on that and it doesn't seem to be the case, perhaps email 
just to me with some reproducible code and I can check further.

Also, out of curiosity, since you are doing two sexes - have you set the 
model up as bipartite or do you just have a nodematch term on sex? I 
don't think that would affect this issue here, but perhaps there's 
something I'm not thinking of.

Cheers,

Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Plotting Specific Ego Network
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Rany -

The "ego" argument should be a list of vertex IDs (i.e., the numbers of 
the vertices you want to select in the adjacency matrix 
representation).? Try using "which" to get the index of the matching 
vertex.? The result is returned as a list, but if you selected only one 
vertex it should have only one entry; just use [[1]] to pull the matrix 
from the list.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Custom constraints (for DAGs)
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I was wondering what possibilities there are for introducing custom 
constraints into statnet.

Long story short, I want to limit the sample space to Directed Acyclic 
Graphs (DAGs). I figured out a way to check whether adding an edge to a 
graph would cause it to stop being a DAG (i.e., add a cycle at any 
length). The attached C++ code creates a 10-by-10 adjacency matrix, and 
only creates edges if they do not create cycles. This is in line with 
the "flipping edges" logic of statnet.

In principle, before "switching on an edge", this could be used to check 
whether the edge introduces cycles, and if it does, to decide to not 
switch it on. However, I have no idea how I could actually implement 
this as a constraint. Is there a way to achieve this through the 
ergm.userterms package?

Best,

Wouter Spekkink

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Shiran,

Your seemingly simple question actually touches many quite fundamental
issues, both statistical and substantive. Let me give you my take, I hope
others in this list will chip in if I miss something.

>From the purely technical point of view, you can fit an ERGM to your
300-node network, take the parameter estimates, and then sample 400-node
networks from an ERGM with the same parameter estimates. HOWEVER, the BIG
question is:

Is it reasonable to assume that the generated 400-node networks can be
thought of as a result of the same real-world process that governs the
observed 300-node network?

The answer is not obvious because it depends how the real-world processes
shaping the network scale with network size. That's a substantive question
and answer depends on what the network represents.

ERGMs with "standard" parametrisation scale with network size preserving
the density, i.e. networks of different sizes sampled from the same ERGM
model (terms and coefficient values) will have on average the same density.
Sometimes this might be what you want, but sometimes it is not. For
example, if you study social network within a school class of 20, kids
might report on average 3 friends. It is not  reasonable to assume that
average number of friends for a kid in a class of 40 will be a double of
that. The average degree will be rather similar. In other words, the
befriending process scales with network size such that average degree
should stay the same and density, as a consequence, decrease. Naive
sampling of bigger networks from the same ERGM will give unrealistically
dense networks. To overcome that offset terms were developed, see:

Krivitsky, Pavel N., Mark S. Handcock, and Martina Morris. "Adjusting for
network size and composition effects in exponential-family random graph
models." *Statistical methodology* 8.4 (2011): 319-339.

Kolaczyk, Eric D., and Pavel N. Krivitsky. "On the question of effective
sample size in network modeling: An asymptotic inquiry." *Statistical
science: a review journal of the Institute of Mathematical Statistics* 30.2
(2015): 184.

... and section 5.3 of

Schweinberger, Michael, Pavel N. Krivitsky, and Carter T. Butts.
"Foundations of Finite-, Super-, and Infinite-Population Random Graph
Inference." *arXiv preprint arXiv:1707.04800* (2017).

You can use offsets with ergm(). I don't have a good code snipet with an
example at this very moment but have a look at ?ergm and arguments `offset`
and `offset.coef`.

 Of course the issue of scaling may not be limited to density vs average
degree (essentially the `edges` term), but may in principle apply to other
terms as well.


hth,
Michal

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM
messages.body_plain:
Dear Shiran,

Could you explain what you mean with grow?


If you want to add, say 250 more nodes and simulate the ties between the
old and new nodeset and within the new nodeset but keeping the ties within
the old nodeset fixed, then this can be easily done with the ergm package.

#1) Add the new nodes to the old network - I assume a simple adjacency
matrix:

# first we create the new bigger network.
#oldNet = your current network with the 300 nodes

newNodes <- 250 #number of new nodes
newSize <- nrow(oldNet) + newNodes

newNet <- matrix(NA, newSize , newSize )
newNet[nrow(oldNet),nrow(oldNet)] <- oldNet

# Now we have and adjacency matrix of the desired size with the former
network between the 300 original nodes and missing data for all other ties

#2) Simulate the new ties -I do not know if you used simulate in R to
simulate the network you have, so I write the script with sufficient
detail, if you have not used it.
# If you are familiar, just set: constraints = ~observed, to keep all old
ties as they are and only simulate the new ones.


newNetSim <- sim (newNet ~ ... , #insert your model parameters here
                               coef = ..., #insert a vector with the
parameter values here
                               statsonly = FALSE,  #to return the simulated
network(s)
                               nsim = 1, # the number of simulated networks
you want
                               constraints = ~observed, #this leaves all
observed ties (here your original network) as they are - the function will
only simulate missing ties
                               control = control.simulate(MCMC.burnin =
1,000,000 #given that your network is very big, I would give the algorithm
enough time to simulate

                                        #through all the cells multiple
times. Maybe your model is quite simple, then a smaller

                                        #value will be fine. Best have a
look at the network statistics of the simulated networks,

                                        #if there are multiple and see if
the simulation is converged

 MCMC.interval = 1,000,000)) # if you sample multiple networks ensure that
they are spaced out far enough in the

                                             # sampling process. Otherwise
your network statistics will be highly correlated.

                                             # Best monitor the auto
correlation of the simulated networks and increase the interval if
necessary.


I hope this helps.

Best Regards,

Robert Krause

University of Groningen
Grote Rozenstraat 31,
Room B119
9712 TG Groningen, The Netherlands

Given the previous comments and suggestions, I'll just add that the 
answer is "yes", subject to the scaling assumption.

WRT "how to":
We used to have a section on this in our ERGM tutorial materials -- it has 
since migrated for the most part to the new ergm.ego tutorial.  But the 
old materials are still online and may be more useful for your case.  You 
can find them here:

https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/raw-attachment/wiki/Sunbelt2016/ergm_tutorial.html#working-with-egocentrically-sampled-network-data

hth,
Martina
